disclaimer: This is an independent portfolio project. It uses publicly available AI use case inventories published by the US Office of Management and Budget (public domain, 17 U.S.C. §105) and the Government of Ontario (Open Government Licence – Ontario), and the UK Government's Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard template (© Crown copyright, Open Government Licence v3.0). Vendor and product names have been removed. Findings describe patterns in the published data and are not claims about any agency's conduct. This is not legal advice. Not affiliated with or endorsed by any government body.

oversight_denominator.heading: Correction, 2026-09-30
oversight_denominator.text: An earlier version of this site counted the nine oversight questions across all 445 entries marked high-impact and reported 317 with none answered. The register's own dictionary asks those nine only of high-impact entries that are deployed. Counted against the 227 entries it does ask, the figure is 101, or 44.5%. The gap is smaller and it is still there. Every other field's denominator was then checked against the dictionary. The same fault was found in the one date field and corrected with it. The check is recorded in governance/corrections.md.

date_denominator.heading: Correction, 2026-09-30
date_denominator.text: The one date field was reported as a share of every row in the register. The dictionary asks for it only of entries at the pilot and deployed stages. Usable dates were published as 31.7% of the register and are 67.6% of the 1480 entries the register asks.

questions.question: How many AI systems are there?
questions.answer: 3,611 are reported one by one. A second route adds 45 agencies reporting against 21 shared tasks. The two count different things and are not added together.
questions.section: The register counts two different kinds of thing

questions.question: Do the published totals agree with the data?
questions.answer: 4 of 7 figures the source states match the file exactly. 3 do not, and the source's own summary table disagrees with the total printed beneath it.
questions.section: Three of the publisher's own figures do not match its data

questions.question: How current is any of it?
questions.answer: No entry records when it was last checked. The register has one date field, asked only of entries at the pilot and deployed stages, readable on 67.6% of those, and it records when a system started running.
questions.section: The register cannot say how current any entry is

questions.question: Can a careful person count this file correctly?
questions.answer: Not without knowing 7 things about how the files are written. Three make a column read fuller than it is, one makes a set of choices look complete, and the rest concern the files themselves.
questions.section: Seven ways a careful person would still get these numbers wrong

elsewhere.question: Could it answer a question about the riskiest systems?
elsewhere.answer: Of 445 entries flagged high-impact, 317 have all nine oversight fields empty.

questions.question: What does another government ask that this one does not?
questions.answer: 8 questions the UK recording standard asks and the US list does not, including who is answerable for the entry, when it was last changed, and whether the system has been retired. Its yes-or-no fields carry an explicit No, and no US oversight answer anywhere records a step as considered and not taken.

findings.question: Is the same AI capability registered once, many times, or folded into something else?
findings.rule_applied: One row is one use case. Candidates are flagged and never merged, and no total is adjusted.
findings.never_summed_reason: The headline count of 3,611 includes nothing from the second route. The two count different things: one counts systems, the other counts an agency ticking a task on a shared list. Adding them would produce a number that means nothing.
findings.caveat: Comparing wording cannot show that two entries are the same system. Entries that read alike may be one system written down twice, or two different systems described in similar words. The count triples depending on how alike they have to be, so it is a choice about where to draw a line rather than something the file contains. All three settings are shown for that reason. Nothing has been merged and no total changed.

findings.question: Does the register hold everything it should, and is each entry filled in?
findings.rule_applied: Completeness is reported within one year only. The earlier inventory is a schema reference and its rows are not read.

completeness_shape.statement: An entry can hold anywhere from none of these fields to all seventeen. Almost every one of those levels occurs somewhere in the list. Inside a single agency, almost every entry sits at the same one or two levels.
completeness_shape.caveat: This counts each entry on its own. No agency average is taken and no agency is compared with another. The pattern describes how information arrives in the file, in the same way the nine oversight fields do, and says nothing about how any agency works.

deployed and piloted.note: The difference of 338 equals exactly the number of rows with no development stage recorded.

total agency submissions.note: No method this project tried reproduced it. The individually reported file names 41 agencies and the consolidated file names 45, and the two write the same agency differently, so any count of distinct submissions depends on a rule for matching them. Eight methods were tried, giving 86, 57 and 52, and every one is recorded in governance/data-provenance.md. A rule that reaches 56 may exist and was not found.

agencies reporting consolidated off-the-.note: The source's own per-agency table and the data file agree at 45. Only the summary bullet differs.

findings.caveat: These figures cannot be compared with the earlier year, because the two years ask different questions: a box left empty in one year may not exist at all in the other. A published list can only show what was declared, so nothing here says anything about systems nobody wrote down. Two fields store an empty answer as a pair of brackets that a spreadsheet counts as an answer, and every figure here treats them as empty. Twenty-two of this register's fields are required only under a condition, so a share of all rows counts entries the question was never put to. Both views are published and the one measured against the entries the register asks is the one that describes an unanswered question. A filled field shows that information was provided, not that the practice is adequate. An empty field is not evidence that the practice is absent.

findings.question: What was done to this data before it was published?
findings.rule_applied: Read from the publisher's own dictionary. Nothing here is inferred.

forms: Computer Vision - AI that processes and interprets visual data (e.g.; images and videos).

findings.caveat: Folding written variants into shared categories is ordinary preparation and is not a criticism of it. It is recorded because the categories a reader counts are the publisher's, not the agencies', and because one published value does not appear in the map that describes them.

findings.question: How old is the information in each entry, and what would trigger a re-check?
findings.rule_applied: Freshness cannot be calculated from this data. The finding replaces the metric.
findings.finding: The register cannot express how current any entry is. It records no verification date, no update date and no review date. Its single date field records when a system became operational, which answers a different question.

operational_date_where_asked.required: Yes, for pilot and deployed use cases.
operational_date_where_asked.statement: Measured against every row, usable dates cover about a third of the register. Measured against the entries the register asks for a date, they cover about two thirds. The second figure is the one that describes a question with no answer. A third of those entries still carry no date that can be read.
operational_date_where_asked.undetermined_note: Entries with no development stage recorded cannot be placed on either side, because the condition is written in terms of stage. They are counted here and in neither of the other two groups.

development_stage_filter.label: Stage is not recency. A stage describes where a system is in its life, not when this entry was last checked.

group_one.statement: Fields touching each of these exist. None records a change, a date of change, or a prior value.

group_two.statement: The degree of autonomy with which a system acts is not present in the 2025 field set. No field touches it at all.

re_verification_trigger_diagnostic.why_reported_separately: No field records a change and no field exists are different statements. Reporting them together would understate the second.

findings.caveat: The one date says when a system started running, not when anyone last looked at its entry. A system running for years might have had its description checked last week or never, and nothing here can tell those apart. Dates written in a form that could mean two different days are not counted, because choosing one reading would invent a precision the file does not have.

findings.question: For every high-impact use case, can the register answer the questions an oversight body would ask?
findings.rule_applied: The subset is the entries labelled high-impact only. Two further bands are labelled separately, using the data's own label.

oversight_conditionality.condition: The publisher's dictionary requires these nine fields "only for high-impact deployed use cases". An entry flagged high-impact but not deployed is not asked them, so a blank there records that the question does not apply, not that it was left unanswered.
oversight_conditionality.statement: Counted across every entry flagged high-impact, the nine are empty on more entries than the register ever asks them of. Counted across the entries the register does ask, the figure is lower and is the one that describes an unanswered question.
oversight_conditionality.caveat: Both figures are in the file. The wider one counts entries the register does not put the question to, so it describes the shape of the register rather than an unanswered question. Neither figure shows whether any oversight practice took place.

oversight_answers.statement: Counting whether these fields are filled and reading what they say give different answers. Most of what is filled in says the work has not finished, and no entry records a step as considered and not taken.
oversight_answers.caveat: These are the words agencies entered. A field saying a step is complete shows that was entered, not that the step was adequate. The absence of any answer recording a step not taken describes the answers present in the file, and the field set offers no wording for one.

oversight_block_shape.statement: The nine oversight fields are answered together or not at all.

withholding_status.dictionary_question: Should this AI use case be withheld from public reporting?
withholding_status.caveat: A blank in a field asking whether something should be withheld is not evidence that anything was withheld. The field is required, so a blank here is different from a blank in a field that did not apply.

presumed_band.dictionary_note: The justification field is specified to appear only when this band is selected, so a low rate in the high-impact band is the specification working.

findings.caveat: A filled field shows that information was provided, not that the practice is adequate. An empty field is not evidence that the practice is absent. The pattern describes what reached the file, not the oversight practice itself. This is a practice exercise modelled on a realistic request. It is not a response to a request from any body.

findings.question: How do real registers differ in what they ask, and what does that reveal about design choices?
findings.rule_applied: Fields asked are compared, never volume. The comparator is the UK recording standard's published template. No UK records are read, so nothing here describes how completely anyone fills it in.

uk_standard.note: Required across UK central government since 2024. The count is of fields the published template asks, not of records anyone filed.

ontario_register.kept_for: One contrast the UK cannot provide: Ontario names no supplier in any published field.

asked_by_the_uk_not_by_the_federal_regis.note: A named person answerable for the entry. The US list records no owner.
When the record was last changed, and when it was retired. The US list has one date and it records when a system started running.

asked_by_the_uk_not_by_the_federal_regis.field: Phase, with Retired among its allowed answers
asked_by_the_uk_not_by_the_federal_regis.note: A published state for a system switched off. The US list has no equivalent, so an entry can only be added.
Where a person sits in the decision. The US list asks this only of its high-impact deployed entries.
What else was weighed and set aside. A record of a decision not taken, which the US oversight fields have no wording for.

asked_by_the_uk_not_by_the_federal_regis.field: Procurement procedure type, and Companies House Number
asked_by_the_uk_not_by_the_federal_regis.note: How the thing was bought and from which registered company. The US list names a supplier and records nothing about the purchase.
How the tool is kept up after it is running.
Which version is in use, so a change to it can be seen.

asked_by_the_federal_register_not_by_the.field: A risk classification with a named threshold
asked_by_the_federal_register_not_by_the.note: The US list flags entries high-impact and asks nine oversight questions of the deployed ones. The UK standard asks every entry the same questions and sets no tier of its own.

asked_by_the_federal_register_not_by_the.field: Whether the entry is withheld from public reporting
asked_by_the_federal_register_not_by_the.note: The US list asks each entry whether it should be withheld. The UK handles this through a separate scope and exemptions policy rather than a field.

published_answers.note: The standard publishes the answers a field may hold. Two matter here. Its yes-or-no fields carry an explicit No, and no US oversight answer anywhere records a step as considered and not taken. And its Phase field carries Retired, so a register built on it can record that a system has stopped, and not only that one exists.

conditionality_is_marked.note: The template marks which fields are asked only under a condition. A reader can therefore tell a question not put from a question unanswered, which is the distinction the US list leaves to whoever reads it.

findings.naming_practice: Three registers, three choices. The US list publishes a supplier name field. The UK standard asks for the supplier and its company registration number. The Ontario list names no supplier in any published field. The supplier field is the one this project removes from its own published data.
findings.caveat: This compares what each register asks. It says nothing about how completely anyone fills any of them in, because no UK records were read. The UK count is of fields in a published template, and a template with more fields is not by itself a better register.
